topline: Four stories today: France's fifth Saturday of cost-of-living and police-bill protests, Paris and Berlin closing in on a deal to make Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos ECB president, ExxonMobil's treaty challenge to the EU's carbon-storage mandate, and Hungary's near-€10bn recovery-fund release under Péter Magyar.

stories.title: France holds a fifth straight Saturday of protests over living costs and a police self-defence bill
stories.summary: Yellow vest, student, education and child-protection groups marched across France on 14 November, the fifth consecutive Saturday of nationwide protests. The interior ministry counted about 106,000 people, including 24,000 in Paris, down from roughly 146,000 a week earlier; organisers claimed 200,000. Police used tear gas in Lyon and Marseille, where a protest ban was defied by about 3,500 people, and some 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed nationwide. Grievances include prices, school funding and a bill giving officers who fire their weapons a presumption of self-defence, backed by Marine Le Pen's party and due in the Senate on 19 November. Unions have called a strike for Tuesday after rejecting a 0.6% minimum-wage rise.
stories.why: Prolonged unrest in the eurozone's second-largest economy complicates France's 2027 budget under the EU excessive-deficit procedure and shapes the run-up to next year's presidential election.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage centres on the breadth of grievances and on alleged police violence, giving protesters' voices most of the space. It notes the lower turnout but stresses that rallies were mostly calm and that the police bill is a key new driver of anger.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Leads with the 100,000-plus turnout and lists affordability, policing and schools as the core complaints.

right.angle: Right-leaning outlets lead with security: intelligence warnings of a radical bloc, the scale of the police deployment and arrests. They stress declining turnout and violence against officers, and give less room to the protesters' complaints about policing.

outlets.name: Le JDD
outlets.note: Pre-march scoop on a confidential police-intelligence note warning of 300–600 radicals and an anti-police tone.

outlets.name: Europe 1
outlets.note: Framed the day around the interior minister's 70,000-strong security deployment.

outlets.name: Brussels Signal
outlets.note: Earlier coverage (2 November): falling turnout and a Molotov attack on a gendarme, tied to France's EU deficit constraints.

stories.differ: The left frames the protests as social anger meeting heavy-handed policing; the right frames them as a fading movement whose main story is public order.

stories.title: France and Germany move toward backing Spain's Hernández de Cos to succeed Lagarde at the ECB
stories.summary: Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos, head of the Bank for International Settlements and former Bank of Spain governor, has emerged as front-runner to succeed Christine Lagarde, who is leaving the ECB early. The Netherlands' Klaas Knot is the other confirmed candidate. Speaking at the Dublin summit on 13 November, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said agreement was in sight but not closed and that he would present Germany's proposal next week after consulting his SPD coalition partners. Press reports describe a package in which Spain takes the presidency, Germany the chief economist post and France keeps market operations. Euro-area leaders aim to settle the choice around their 26 November meeting, with a formal decision by year-end.
stories.why: The next ECB president will steer monetary policy for 20 eurozone countries for eight years, and the package deal shows how the big capitals divide top EU jobs.

left.angle: No distinct left-leaning take on this round of talks was found in today's searches; coverage so far is mostly from straight-news and business outlets.

right.angle: Centre-right business coverage in Germany focuses on Berlin's leverage: Merz's timing, his need to square the SPD, and securing a heavyweight German seat such as chief economist rather than the presidency itself.

outlets.name: Handelsblatt
outlets.note: Leads with Merz promising a German proposal next week and stresses the deal is not yet done.

stories.differ: With no clear left-leaning take, the contrast is limited; German business coverage treats the race as a negotiation over posts, while Spanish media emphasise the chance of a Spanish president.

stories.title: ExxonMobil launches treaty arbitration against the EU's carbon-storage obligation
stories.summary: Three ExxonMobil entities have filed a notice of arbitration against the EU under the Energy Charter Treaty, challenging the Net-Zero Industry Act's requirement that major oil and gas producers help build 50 million tonnes a year of CO2 injection capacity by 2030. According to a Commission document reported by Euronews, the companies argue the target is unachievable because of permitting delays and costs, and allege breaches of fair treatment, non-discrimination and expropriation protections. They plan to seek interim measures suspending the obligation for their subsidiaries. The EU and UK have left the treaty, but its 20-year sunset clause still protects existing investments. The Commission declined to comment on an ongoing case.
stories.why: The case tests whether a flagship EU climate-industry law can be slowed by investor-state arbitration, and revives debate over neutralising the Energy Charter Treaty's sunset clause.

left.angle: Left-leaning and campaign coverage folds the case into a wider critique of investor-state dispute settlement, leading with the hundreds of billions fossil-fuel firms have claimed from governments and calling for such treaties to be scrapped.

outlets.name: Common Dreams
outlets.note: Cites ExxonMobil's EU claim as an example of fossil-fuel firms using ISDS against climate rules, timed to COP31.

right.angle: No right-leaning take on the ExxonMobil filing was found in today's searches.

stories.differ: Only one side has engaged so far: the left sees corporate abuse of a discredited treaty, while industry's case that the target is unrealistic is aired mainly in trade and straight-news reporting.

stories.title: Commission prepares to release almost €10bn in recovery funds to Hungary
stories.summary: The European Commission is set to approve nearly all of Hungary's roughly €10bn Recovery and Resilience Facility allocation, officials told Euronews, with an assessment possible as soon as next week and payments due to be authorised by the end of November. The money was frozen under Viktor Orbán; Péter Magyar's government, elected in April, agreed a €16.4bn unfreezing deal with Ursula von der Leyen in May and says it has met 27 'super milestones' after amending more than 100 laws. Hungary's revised plan shifted €3.6bn into capital for a state development bank and a state rolling-stock company. Member states must still sign off, and €2.2bn tied to academic freedom and LGBTI conditions remains blocked.
stories.why: It would be the clearest sign yet that the EU's conditionality tools can be reversed after reforms, and a test of how strictly Brussels checks milestones under deadline pressure.

left.angle: No fresh left-leaning take on this week's reports was found. Earlier centre-left coverage framed the unfreezing as a reward for Magyar's anti-corruption reforms and a credibility test for the EU.

outlets.name: EUobserver
outlets.note: Earlier coverage (23 September) of the €4.2bn cohesion release, stressing reform progress.

right.angle: Conservative outlets close to Hungary's former governing camp stress conditionality and tight deadlines, and question whether the new government's record matches Brussels' praise; one headline says approval came despite fresh rule-of-law concerns.

outlets.name: The European Conservative
outlets.note: Headline frames EU approval as coming despite new rule-of-law worries (page could not be read).

outlets.name: Hungarian Conservative
outlets.note: Earlier coverage (10 July) of ECOFIN approval, highlighting strict conditions and Fidesz criticism of the new government.

stories.differ: Centre-left coverage treats the money as earned by reform; right-leaning coverage questions whether Brussels is applying the same standards to Magyar that it applied to Orbán.
